# Motivation

## Questions

Suppose you wrote some code:

- a script that parses and cleans some data set
- an analysis script
- a new algorithm
- a package

::: {.poll .fragment}
Who owns the code? <br>
What can you or others do with it?
:::


## Questions

In addition to code, suppose you also:

- collected data,
- generated derived information (tables, summaries)
- created various plots,
- wrote a report,

::: {.poll .fragment}
Who owns all of these? <br>
What can you or others do with them?
:::


# Introduction

## Did you know?

. . .

\

Any software you write (and save)

- is [copyright on creation]{.bold-hilit}
- you don't have to do any special to claim copyright


## What is Copyright?

. . .

It's a legal process that grants the creator of an original work
[exclusive rights to its use and distribution]{.bold-hilit}

- Under international law, copyright applies automatically the moment an 
original work is "fixed in a tangible medium."

- The second someone types code into a text file and saves it (or pushes it to GitHub), 
they own the copyright to that exact expression of code.

-  A creator does not need to include the © symbol, write "All Rights Reserved," 
or register with a government office to be protected.


## Owner of Copyright

::: {.poll}
Who is the owner of the copyright?
:::

\

. . .

The copyright owner may be [you, or your employer]{.bold-hilit}

. . .

\

[Exception:]{.bold-hilit} works created by the US government cannot be copyrighted
(they are considered to be in the _public domain_)


## Copyright and Software

\

Regarding software, we care about rights of:

- Reproduction
- Distribution
- Modification
- Derivative works

. . .

Similar considerations can apply to creative-data and media (e.g. reports, 
graphics, summaries, audio, video)


## Four Main Rights

Copyright (_All Rights Reserved_) means a stranger cannot legally do any of the 
following without explicit, written permission from the owner:

- [Reproduce:]{.bold-hilit} They cannot download, copy, or duplicate the file 
onto their local machine.

- [Distribute:]{.bold-hilit} They cannot host the file on their own server 
or share it with others.

- [Modify:]{.bold-hilit} They cannot change a single line of the code to fix 
a bug or tweak an algorithm.

- [Derive:]{.bold-hilit} They cannot build a new software package that imports 
or relies on that copyrighted code.


## Data-Code-Media under Copyright Law

\

Copyright is a critical nuance for computational reproducibility

\

### Why?

Because reproducibility involves code, data, and derived outputs 
(tables, graphics, summaries, etc). 


## The Paradox of Public Repositories

This creates a massive legal trap on platforms like GitHub.

- [Public to View -vs- Public to Use:]{.bold-hilit} Making a repository 
"Public" on GitHub means people have a license to view and fork the code 
on GitHub's infrastructure (per GitHub's Terms of Service).

- [Invisible Wall:]{.bold-hilit} It does not grant viewers the right to 
download it, run it on their university cluster, 
or use it in their research paper.

- [Without a license file, a public repository is looking glass science.]{.bold-hilit} 
Strangers can look at it, but if they touch it, they are technically committing copyright infringement.

- [The Reproducibility Failure:]{.bold-hilit} If a peer cannot legally run 
your code, your computational science is not reproducible.


## Code vs. Data under Copyright Law

To further complicate things, copyright treats code, data, and media
completely differently:

- [Code is protected:]{.bold-hilit} Copyright treats software code exactly 
like literary work (like a novel or a poem).

- [Media is also protected:]{.bold-hilit} Reports, graphics, audio, video 
are creative work.

- [Facts and Data are NOT protected:]{.bold-hilit} Copyright does not protect 
facts, ideas, mathematical formulas, or raw data. For example, a table listing 
the boiling points of elements cannot be copyrighted because those are facts.

- [Creativity in Data:]{.bold-hilit} Only the creative arrangement or 
original selection of a dataset can be copyrighted (e.g., a carefully 
curated and cleaned database structure).


## Example: Data of Coffee Shops in the Bay Area

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
[Facts]{.mdlit}

- names
- street addresses
- phone numbers
- operating hours 

::: {.fragment}
Anyone is legally free to scrape 
that public data and publish it.
:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment}
[Copyrighted data]{.hilit}

::: {.fragment}
A selective, expert-curated guidebook or specialized database, 
such as _The 50 Best Independent Coffee Shops in the Bay Area_.
:::

- Original Selection
- Creative arrangement
:::
::::


## Example: Data of Coffee Shops in the Bay Area

::: {.poll}
_The 50 Best Independent Coffee Shops in the Bay Area_
:::

- No one can legally prevent you from reusing the individual facts 
(e.g., that a specific café is located at 123 Main Street)

- However, the specific selection, arrangement, and editorial presentation 
created by the author are protected by copyright. 

- Copying the entire curated list or 
database layout as your own would constitute copyright infringement.


# Software Licenses

## Software Licensing Spectrum

1) [All Rights Reserved]{.hilit}
2) Proprietary licenses (closed)
3) Permissive Licenses (the "Do Whatever" Category)
4) Copyleft / Viral Licenses (the "Keep It Free" Category)
5) [Public Domain]{.mdlit}

. . .

Resources: 

::: {.nonincremental}
- Free Software Foundation: <https://www.fsf.org/>
- Open Source Initiative: <https://opensource.org/>
:::


## Questions

\

::: {.poll}
What do you understand by "Free Software"?
:::

::: {.poll .fragment}
What do you understand by "Open Source"?
:::


## Public Domain

There is no official "public domain license" because a work in the 
public domain belongs to everyone rather than being owned or 
restricted by a license.

\

However, tools and public-domain-equivalent instruments exist to 
legally dedicate or waive copyright, e.g.

[0BSD (Zero-Clause BSD):]{.bold-hilit} A license that grants unconditional 
permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute a work without any attribution requirement.


## Permissive Licenses 

The ["Do Whatever"]{.mdlit} Category

- [MIT License:]{.bold-hilit} Short, simple, allows commercial use, requires keeping the copyright notice.

- [BSD License:]{.bold-hilit} Like MIT but with multiple variants depending on the number of clauses.

- [Apache 2.0:]{.bold-hilit} Similar to MIT but includes explicit patent rights protection from contributors.

- [Best For:]{.bold-hilit} Maximizing adoption, industry collaboration, and academic software packages.


## Permissive Licenses (cont'd)

They allow you to freely use, modify, and distribute software for commercial 
or private use without requiring you to open-source your derivative code.

- [Permissive Freedom:]{.bold-hilit} Allow free use, copying, modification, 
and integration into proprietary (closed-source) software.

- [No Copyleft:]{.bold-hilit} They are not ["viral"]{.hilit} like the GPL; you are not 
forced to release your modified source code under the same license.

- [Attribution & Disclaimers:]{.bold-hilit} They require you to keep the 
original copyright notice, license text, and liability disclaimers intact.


## Permissive Licenses (cont'd) {.smaller}

\

| Feature                        | MIT | BSD (2-Clause) | BSD (3-Clause) | Apache |
|--------------------------------|-----|----------------|----------------|--------|
| Document Length                | Short |	Short	    | Short          | Long |
| Commercial Use Allowed         | Yes |	Yes	        | Yes            | Yes |
| Modification & Distribution    | Yes |	Yes	        | Yes            | Yes |
| Requires Copyright Attribution | Yes |	Yes	        | Yes            | Yes |
| Non-Endorsement Clause         | No  |	No	        | Yes            | Yes |
| Explicit Patent Grant          | No  |	No	        | No             | Yes |
| Explicit Trademark Protection  | No  |	No	        | Yes            | Yes |
| Requires Stating Changes       | No  |	No	        | No             | Yes |


## Copyleft / Viral Licenses 

\

The ["Keep It Free"]{.hilit} Category[^1]

- [GNU GPL v3:]{.bold-hilit} Anyone who modifies and redistributes the code must 
also open-source their changes under GPL.

. . .

Keep in mind that this type of licenses can deter commercial partners or integration 
into proprietary institutional tools.

[^1]: Free as in freedom, not as in cost or price.


## Limitation of Software Licenses

Software licenses do not fit:

- text
- figures
- trained weights
- tabular data
- (media in general)

. . .

Instead of software licenses you need to use Creative Commons (CC) Framework


## Functional vs. Static Expression

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
[Software Licenses]{.bold-hilit}

These assume the work will be compiled, executed, linked, or 
imported into other programs. 

They regulate things like running the code, modifying the source logic, 
or embedding the code into a larger application.
:::

::: {.column .fragment}
[Media Licenses]{.bold-hilit}

These assume the work will be read, viewed, listened to, or displayed. 

They regulate things like printing a text, showing an image in a presentation, 
or remixing an audio track into a video.
:::
::::


## Limitation of Software Licenses

- If you apply a software license to a research paper 
or an image, it is legally muddy. 

- Concepts like "compiling" or "linking" do not map onto a JPEG or 
a PDF or MP3 or MP4 files.

- Software licenses generally assume the asset is a functional tool, 
not an artistic expression.


## The Threat of "Non-Commercial" (NC) Clauses in Science

Students often instinctively gravitate toward 
[Creative Commons Non-Commercial (CC BY-NC)]{.bold-hilit} for their 
research papers, figures, and slide decks because they want to protect 
their work from being sold by corporations.

However, NC clauses are dangerous for open science. 


## NC clauses (cont'd)

NC clauses are dangerous for open science, because:

- "Commercial use" is poorly defined in court. 

- [Academic Trap:]{.bold-hilit} If a researcher at a private university or a commercial 
medical center downloads a dataset under a CC BY-NC license to reproduce 
a study, they might be violating the license because their institution 
charges tuition or holds patents.

- [Funding Compliance:]{.bold-hilit} Many public grants (like NIH or Horizon Europe) 
strictly mandate that research outputs be published under CC BY 
(Attribution Only) or CC0 (Public Domain) to maximize public good. 
An NC clause will often violate funding terms.


# Recommendations


## Best Practices Checklist for a Project Repository

Every repository needs a root-level `LICENSE` file. You can split your repository 
assets using the correct legal tool for each job:

- 💻 The Code (Python/R script files, Notebooks): 
Use MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0, or GPL v3.

- 📊 The Data (CSV files, SQL databases, JSON logs): 
Use CC0 (Public Domain Dedication) to avoid legal bottlenecks when combining datasets.

- 📝 The Narrative (Research papers, README text, documentation pages): 
Use CC BY 4.0.

- 🎨 The Visuals (Plots, diagrams, summary charts, introductory videos): 
Use CC BY 4.0.


## Option 1) The Multi-License README file

Using a `LICENSE` file, and a `README.md` file

- Keep one primary `LICENSE` file in the root directory
    + File Name: `LICENSE` (No extension)
    + Contents: Full text of the primary software license (e.g., the MIT License).
- At the very bottom of the `README.md`, students add a "License & Citation" section that explicitly draws boundaries around the assets.


## Option 1) The Multi-License README file

At the very bottom of the `README.md` include some text like the following:

::: {.small}
```{.markdown filename="README.md" code-line-numbers="false"}
## Licensing

The assets in this repository are split under different licenses 
to ensure maximum reproducibility:

- **Code:** All source code (`.py`, `.sh`, `.ipynb`) is licensed under 
the [MIT License](LICENSE).

- **Data:** All datasets in the `/data` directory are dedicated to the 
public domain under [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org).

- **Narrative & Visuals:** All documentation, text, and figures 
(`/plots`, `/docs`) are licensed under a 
[Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org).
```
:::


## Option 2) The REUSE Standard

The REUSE standard explicitly tags every single asset using a dedicated 
directory and small text headers.

Instead of putting licenses in the root directory, you create a folder named 
`LICENSES/` and place the text of every license they use inside it, 
named exactly after their SPDX identifier:

- `LICENSES/MIT.txt`
- `LICENSES/CC0-1.0.txt`
- `LICENSES/CC-BY-4.0.txt`


## Option 2) The REUSE Standard

Add a tiny, commented header to the top of your files to state who 
owns it and how it is licensed.

```{.markdown filename="script.py" code-line-numbers="false"}
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Your Name <your.email@university.edu>
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
```

\

```{.markdown filename="paper.qmd" code-line-numbers="false"}
<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Your Name <your.email@university.edu>
SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0
-->
```


# Citation

## About Citation

In addition to a top-level README file, as well as LICENSE files 
(for code and non-code) it's a good idea to have a CITATION file.

- Citation File Format (CITATION.cff)

- This YAML file lets platforms like GitHub automatically generate 
APA/BibTeX citations for repositories.

- Also, you can mint a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) by linking 
a GitHub release to Zenodo.


## Citation example {.smaller}

```{.markdown filename="CITATION.cff" code-line-numbers="false"}
cff-version: 1.2.0
message: "If you use this software, please cite it as below."
authors:
  - family-names: "Smith"
    given-names: "Jane"
    orcid: "https://orcid.org"
  - family-names: "Doe"
    given-names: "John"
title: "My Awesome Data Science Tool"
version: "1.4.2"
doi: "10.5281/zenodo.1234567"
date-released: "2026-10-15"
url: "https://project-webpage.com"
repository-code: "https://github.com/project-repo"
keywords:
  - "data-science"
  - "programming"
license: "MIT"
```
